metadata.title: How to Build an AI Product from Scratch
metadata.greeting_note: Presenter: Vineet S.. Closing card: MedhavyOutro (toolkit defaults).
metadata.note: General explainer from standard product-development practice; no statistics, versions or sources claimed. Support-team scenario is illustrative.

beats.narration_text: Hello, I'm Vineet S.. Most people building an AI product start with the model. That is backwards. Let's walk the whole lifecycle, from a blank page to a product people actually use.

props.segment: How to Build an AI Product from Scratch
props.command: How do I build an AI product from scratch?
output: Seven stages, and the last one loops back
Start small, prove it, then grow

beats.narration_text: Building an AI product starts with a real problem and one small test. Not a giant model, not a mountain of data. You earn the right to build more by proving the smallest version works for real people.

props.text:
Building an AI product
starts with a model
and a lot of data.
props.triggerWords: a model, a lot of data
props.replacementWords: a real problem, one small test

beats.narration_text: Here are the seven stages. Problem. Users. Use case. Minimum viable product. Evaluation. Launch. And improvement. Notice the shape: it is a loop, not a line. What you learn after launch sends you back to the start.

The first three stages happen before any code. Name the problem: what hurts, for whom, and how often. Then understand the users: watch how they really work, not how they say they work. Then define one narrow use case, with clear inputs and outputs.

layers.title: Problem
layers.sub: What hurts, for whom, how often

layers.title: Users
layers.sub: Watch the real workflow, not the described one

layers.title: Use case
layers.sub: One narrow job, clear inputs and outputs

beats.narration_text: Take an example. A support team is drowning in tickets. That is the problem. Interviews and ticket history show the users, and what they repeat all day. The use case is narrow: draft a reply, and a human approves it. Not replace the team. Draft, then approve.

Now the minimum viable product. The smallest version that tests your biggest risk. You can fake it first, with a human behind the curtain. Use an existing model before training your own. Test on a small set of real examples, with one small group of users.

layers.title: Real examples
layers.sub: A small set from real work

beats.narration_text: Then evaluate, and try to prove yourself wrong. Build a test set from real cases. Measure accuracy where mistakes cost the most. Read the failures one by one. Ask users what they actually did with the answer. And check cost and speed, because a correct answer that is too slow still fails.

Launch small. Release to a limited group first, watch quality as the world changes, and learn from feedback. Then improve: adjust the prompt, the data, or the model, and go around again. Launch is not the finish line. It is where the real learning begins.

layers.title: Watch quality
layers.sub: Models drift as the world changes

beats.narration_text: So, building an AI product. Start with a real problem. Understand the people who have it. Define one narrow use case. Build the smallest version and evaluate it honestly. Launch small, then keep improving.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. I want to build an AI product for this problem: [describe it]. Walk me through who the users are, one narrow use case, the smallest MVP I could test this month, how I would evaluate it using ten real examples, and which small group should see it first. Then tell me the biggest reason it might fail. The last sentence is the important one. Every product has a most likely way to fail, and finding it before you build is the cheapest test there is. Fill in your own problem, and see whether Claude's answer changes what you build first. Pause here and run it.
